description: We are FSM StarShell, a technology team founded by students from Fatih Sultan Mehmet Vakıf University (FSMVÜ) with a deep passion for science, engineering, and space exploration. Our focus is on utilizing programming, artificial intelligence, and engineering to create smart, scalable solutions for real-world and extraterrestrial challenges. By combining our academic foundation with rapid prototyping skills, we love turning our curiosity into innovative projects for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
Core Logic & Terrain: Pure JavaScript code (unit-tested in Node) that computes slopes using the Horn (1981) 3x3 method and generates Lambertian hillshades.

Routing & Movement: Implements an 8-neighbor grid graph subject to slope and boulder clearance constraints. Walking times are calculated using Tobler’s asymmetric hiking function, adjusted by suit mobility and soil softness (thermal inertia). Dijkstra's algorithm handles travel times and return-to-habitat margins.

Stop Optimization & Safety: Optimizes visiting order using branch-and-bound (exact up to 7 stops, nearest-neighbor beyond). Safety margins are evaluated against EVA limits to determine GO, CAUTION, or NO-GO verdicts based on time margins, steep terrain percentages, and destination reachability.

Space Weather & Radiation: Calculates radiation doses factoring in real-time NOAA SWPC proton flux data (>10 MeV) with a graceful manual selection fallback.

3D Visualizations: WebGL-based globe and terrain views built on Three.js (with classic-script fallbacks for file:// compatibility). They render real DEM heightmap data and route paths accurately with graceful degradation when WebGL is unavailable.
details:
What it does. MarsWalk Atlas turns decades of robotic Mars mapping into a tool a human explorer can actually walk with. It layers six real NASA datasets over one hyper-local map — HiRISE elevation with multi-scale hillshade, derived slope hazard, a boulder mask with clearance buffer,

TES thermal inertia (soft ground), USGS SIM 3292 geology, and the co-registered HiRISE orthophoto — then plans a complete extravehicular activity (EVA): pick science stops (or click the map to add your own), press one button, and the tool finds the best visiting order and a walking

route that avoids too-steep ground and boulders, slows down on soft sand, and respects a suited astronaut's mobility. The distance of every leg between stops is written directly on the route line, so the crew reads the plan like a trekking map.

How it works. The terrain becomes an 8-connected grid graph; hazardous cells are removed (slope limit, boulder buffer, no corner-cutting, per-step slope rule) and Dijkstra — with a binary heap — searches on walking time, not distance: Tobler's hiking function × suit mobility factor ×

soft-ground penalty. Because that cost is asymmetric, a second reverse search precomputes the time home from every cell. That field powers the project's core safety metric, the return margin: at any point on the route, margin = EVA limit − (elapsed time + walk-home-from-here). A

negative margin anywhere makes the plan NO-GO; under 30 minutes, CAUTION. The astronaut display adds remaining oxygen, radiation dose scaled by a live NOAA SWPC space-weather feed, and an ABORT banner at the point the margin runs out. A 3D globe (real MOLA displacement — Olympus Mons,

Valles Marineris and Hellas are tangibly visible, with click-to-fly feature labels) lets the crew pick any region of Mars and load a real-data grid on demand; a rotatable 3D terrain view and a helmet-visor HUD mode with a walkable simulation complete the loop from orbit down to

bootsteps.

Benefits & impact. NASA's Mars data exists at global and regional scales; a Marswalk needs street-level, route-level planning with safety first. Every number shown is traceable: data sources, processing commands and honest caveats (which layers are proxies, which parameters are

editable assumptions) are documented in the app and the repository — building trust, not just visuals.

Tools & software. Vanilla HTML/JavaScript/Python, no build step, fully offline (Leaflet BSD-2, three.js r165 MIT and the Big Shoulders font OFL — all bundled). GDAL + NumPy data pipeline; a Python-stdlib on-demand area server for any region; bilingual EN/TR interface; 38 automated

tests (11 JavaScript + 27 Python), including elevation checks against Olympus Mons and Hellas.

Creativity & considerations. The return margin reframes routing as a consumables problem — "if I turn back now, do I make it home?" The honest-assumption design invites crews to adjust every parameter and see the verdict update live. Graceful degradation (3D → flat map, live → manual

space weather, server → offline Python command) keeps it working anywhere: a habitat tablet, a laptop, or a judges' offline zip. We deliberately chose Curiosity's 2025 boxwork campaign on Mount Sharp as the study area, so every stop has a real science goal and real point-of-view imagery from the location.
